paper.title: Expected TGT paper 5 · balanced
paper.source: Written by GS HOUSE for the UP TGT Mathematics exam expected in December 2026, in the pattern of the UP TGT paper of 3 June 2026 and the official syllabus: 28 questions asked in earlier papers (16 from UP TGT 2003 and 12 from UP TGT 2001; each solved again, misprints repaired) and 62 new; every question checked by a second mathematician

src.label: Expected TGT 5 · Q1 · asked in UP TGT 2003

en.q: The value of $\int \dfrac{a^{\sqrt x}}{\sqrt x}\,dx$ is:
en.explanation:
Put $\sqrt x = t$, so $\frac{dx}{2\sqrt x} = dt$, i.e. $\frac{dx}{\sqrt x} = 2\,dt$.
Then $\int \frac{a^{\sqrt x}}{\sqrt x}dx = 2\int a^t\,dt = \frac{2a^t}{\log_e a} + C = 2a^{\sqrt x}\log_a e + C$, because $\frac{1}{\log_e a} = \log_a e$.
notes: Factor 2 lost, and $\log_e a$ multiplied where it should divide.
$\log_{10} e$ would belong to base 10, not base $a$.
Multiplies by $\log_e a$ (as in $\frac{d}{dx}a^x$) instead of dividing.
facts: $\int a^x\,dx = \frac{a^x}{\log_e a} + C = a^x\log_a e + C$.

src.label: Expected TGT 5 · Q2 · asked in UP TGT 2003

en.q: If one of the lines of the pair $ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 = 0$ bisects the angle between the positive directions of the axes, then $a, b, h$ satisfy the relation:
en.explanation:
The bisector of the positive axes is $y = x$. A line $y = mx$ belongs to the pair iff $a + 2hm + bm^2 = 0$; with $m = 1$: $a + 2h + b = 0$, i.e. $a + b = -2h$.
Example: $(y - x)(y + 3x) = -3x^2 + 2xy + y^2$ gives $a = -3$, $h = 1$, $b = 1$ and $a + b = -2 = -2h$.
notes: $y = x$ lies on the pair: $a + 2h + b = 0$.
Fails for the same example: $a - b = -4$.
True only when $h \le 0$; fails for $y = x$, $y = -3x$ ($a = -3, h = 1, b = 1$).
facts: $y = mx$ is one of the lines $ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 = 0$ iff $bm^2 + 2hm + a = 0$.

src.label: Expected TGT 5 · Q3 · asked in UP TGT 2001

en.q: A merchant sells a pen for ₹24.00. The trader makes a percentage profit equal to the cost price of the pen. What will be the cost price of the pen?
en.explanation:
Let the cost price be ₹$x$. The profit is $x\%$ of $x$, i.e. $\frac{x^2}{100}$.
$$x + \frac{x^2}{100} = 24 \Rightarrow x^2 + 100x - 2400 = 0 \Rightarrow (x + 120)(x - 20) = 0.$$
So $x = 20$ (the negative root is rejected). Check: $20\%$ of ₹20 is ₹4 and $20 + 4 = 24$.
path: 17.4 Banking, shares, profit and loss, taxation
facts: $SP = CP\left(1 + \frac{p}{100}\right)$; when the profit per cent equals the cost price, solve $x + \frac{x^2}{100} = SP$.

en.q: A wheel makes 360 revolutions in one minute. Through how many radians does it turn in one second?
en.explanation: 360 revolutions per minute is $\frac{360}{60} = 6$ revolutions per second. One revolution is $2\pi$ radians, so in one second the wheel turns $6 \times 2\pi = 12\pi$ radians.
notes: $\pi$ radians per revolution used in place of $2\pi$.
That is the angle turned in one minute.
path: 9.1 Trigonometric ratios and the unit circle
facts: One revolution $= 360^\circ = 2\pi$ radians; $1$ radian $= \frac{180^\circ}{\pi}$.

en.q: If $A$ is a $3 \times 4$ matrix and $B$ is a matrix such that both $A^TB$ and $BA^T$ are defined, then the order of $B$ is:
en.explanation: $A^T$ is $4 \times 3$. For $A^TB$ to be defined, $B$ must have 3 rows (the number of columns of $A^T$); for $BA^T$ to be defined, $B$ must have 4 columns (the number of rows of $A^T$). So $B$ is $3 \times 4$, the same order as $A$.
notes: Correct: 3 rows for $A^TB$ and 4 columns for $BA^T$.
That is the order of $A^T$; then neither product is defined.
Makes $A^TB$ defined, but $BA^T$ needs $B$ to have 4 columns.
Makes $BA^T$ defined, but $A^TB$ needs $B$ to have 3 rows.
facts: $PQ$ is defined when the number of columns of $P$ equals the number of rows of $Q$; an $m \times n$ matrix times an $n \times p$ matrix is $m \times p$.

src.label: Expected TGT 5 · Q6 · asked in UP TGT 2001

en.q: The mean of the following data is 50: class intervals 0–20, 20–40, 40–60, 60–80, 80–100 with frequencies 17, $f_2$, 32, $f_4$, 19 (total 120). Then $f_2$ and $f_4$ will be:
facts: Two missing frequencies need two equations: $\sum f = N$ and $\sum fx = N\bar x$.

src.label: Expected TGT 5 · Q7 · asked in UP TGT 2003

en.q: Area bounded by the curve $y = x\sin x$ and the $x$-axis, where $x = 0$ to $x = 2\pi$, is:
en.explanation:
$\int x\sin x\,dx = -x\cos x + \sin x$. The curve is above the axis on $(0, \pi)$ and below it on $(\pi, 2\pi)$.
$\int_0^{\pi} x\sin x\,dx = \pi$; $\int_{\pi}^{2\pi} x\sin x\,dx = -2\pi - \pi = -3\pi$.
Area $= \pi + |-3\pi| = 4\pi$.
notes: Size of the signed integral $\int_0^{2\pi} x\sin x\,dx = -2\pi$.
facts: Area $= \int |y|\,dx$: split the interval where the curve crosses the axis.

en.q: The number of common tangents to two circles which touch each other externally is:
en.explanation: Two direct (external) common tangents, and the two transverse tangents merge into the single common tangent at the point of contact: 3 in all.
notes: Forgets the tangent at the point of contact.
That is for two circles lying outside each other.
Two direct tangents and the tangent at the point of contact.
That is for circles touching internally.
facts: Common tangents of two circles: 4 (apart), 3 (touching externally), 2 (cutting), 1 (touching internally), 0 (one inside the other).

en.q: The volume of a sphere of radius 21 cm is (use $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$):
en.explanation: $V = \frac43\pi r^3 = \frac43 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 21 \times 21 \times 21 = 4 \times 22 \times 441 = 38808$ cm³.
notes: That is the surface area $4\pi r^2$ (in cm²).
That is the volume of a hemisphere.
$\frac43\pi r^2$: radius squared instead of cubed.
facts: Sphere: $V = \frac43\pi r^3$, $S = 4\pi r^2$; hemisphere: $V = \frac23\pi r^3$, total surface $3\pi r^2$.

en.q: The centre $Z(G) = \{z \in G : zg = gz \text{ for all } g \in G\}$ of a group $G$ is:
en.explanation: $e \in Z(G)$. If $z, w \in Z(G)$, then $w^{-1}g = gw^{-1}$ for all $g$, so $(zw^{-1})g = z(gw^{-1}) = (gz)w^{-1} = g(zw^{-1})$: $zw^{-1} \in Z(G)$, and $Z(G)$ is a subgroup. Its elements commute with every element of $G$, in particular with each other, so it is abelian.
notes: Its elements commute with all of $G$, hence with each other.
Only when $G$ is abelian; the centre of $S_3$ is $\{e\}$.
facts: $Z(G)$ is an abelian (indeed normal) subgroup of $G$; $Z(G) = G$ exactly when $G$ is abelian.

en.q: The general fertility rate (GFR) of a region for a year is the number of live births in that year per 1000 of the:
en.explanation: GFR $= \dfrac{\text{live births in the year}}{\text{women aged 15–49}} \times 1000$. The crude birth rate uses the whole mid-year population instead.
notes: That base gives the crude birth rate.
Only women who can bear children are counted.
facts: Crude birth and death rates use the mid-year population; GFR uses women aged 15–49; IMR uses the live births of the year.

src.label: Expected TGT 5 · Q13 · asked in UP TGT 2001

en.q: The circle $x^2 + y^2 + 4x - 7y + 12 = 0$ intersects the $y$-axis; then the length of the intercepted portion is:
en.explanation: Put $x = 0$: $y^2 - 7y + 12 = 0 \Rightarrow y = 3, 4$. Intercept $= 4 - 3 = 1$. (Formula: $2\sqrt{f^2 - c} = 2\sqrt{\frac{49}{4} - 12} = 1$.)
facts: The $y$-intercept of $x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0$ is $2\sqrt{f^2 - c}$.

en.q: The general solution of a differential equation of order $n$ contains:
en.explanation: Solving an equation of order $n$ needs $n$ integrations, each bringing one constant; so the general solution has $n$ independent arbitrary constants. E.g. $y'' + y = 0$ (order 2) has $y = A\cos x + B\sin x$.
facts: Order of the DE = number of independent arbitrary constants in its general solution; a particular solution has none.

en.q: $\tanh x$ is equal to:
en.explanation: $\tanh x = \dfrac{\sinh x}{\cosh x} = \dfrac{e^x - e^{-x}}{e^x + e^{-x}}$; multiplying numerator and denominator by $e^x$ gives $\dfrac{e^{2x} - 1}{e^{2x} + 1}$.
facts: $\sinh x = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2}$, $\cosh x = \frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2}$, $\tanh x = \frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x}$, and $-1 < \tanh x < 1$.

en.q: A particle is projected with a velocity of 20 m/s at an angle of 15° to the horizontal. Taking $g = 10$ m/s², its horizontal range is:
en.explanation: $R = \dfrac{u^2\sin 2\alpha}{g} = \dfrac{400 \times \sin 30^\circ}{10} = \dfrac{400 \times \frac12}{10} = 20$ m.
facts: $R = \frac{u^2\sin2\alpha}{g}$: equal for $\alpha$ and $90^\circ - \alpha$, greatest ($\frac{u^2}{g}$) at $45^\circ$.

en.q: If $[x]$ denotes the greatest integer not exceeding $x$, then $\lim_{x\to 2^-} [x]$ is:
en.explanation: For $1 \le x < 2$, $[x] = 1$, so the left-hand limit at 2 is 1. The right-hand limit is 2, so $\lim_{x\to2}[x]$ itself does not exist.
notes: The one-sided limit exists; only the two-sided one fails.
facts: At an integer $n$: left limit of $[x]$ is $n - 1$, right limit is $n$ (a jump).

src.label: Expected TGT 5 · Q18 · asked in UP TGT 2001

en.q: The sum of the series $\log_4 2 - \log_8 2 + \log_{16} 2 - \dots$ is:
en.explanation:
$\log_{2^k} 2 = \frac1k$, so the series is $\frac12 - \frac13 + \frac14 - \frac15 + \dots$.
Since $\log_e 2 = 1 - \frac12 + \frac13 - \frac14 + \dots$, the series equals $1 - \log_e 2$.
notes: Sign of the log term taken wrongly.
Negative, but the series is positive (its first term $\frac12$ exceeds the second).
That is $1 - \frac12 + \frac13 - \dots$, which starts one term earlier.
facts: $\log_e(1 + x) = x - \frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{x^3}{3} - \dots$; at $x = 1$ it gives $\log_e 2$.

src.label: Expected TGT 5 · Q19 · asked in UP TGT 2003

en.q: $ABC$ is a uniform triangular lamina with centre of gravity $G$. If the portion $GBC$ is removed, the centre of gravity of the remaining portion is at $G'$. Then $GG'$ is equal to:
en.explanation:
Let $D$ be the mid-point of $BC$, so $AG = 2GD$. $\triangle GBC$ has $\frac13$ of the area; its centre $G_1$ lies on $GD$ with $GG_1 = \frac23 GD = \frac13 AG$.
The remaining part ($\frac23$ of the weight) has its centre $G'$ on the other side of $G$, with $\frac23 W \cdot GG' = \frac13 W \cdot GG_1$.
So $GG' = \frac12 \cdot \frac13 AG = \frac16 AG$.
notes: That is $GG_1$, the shift of the removed part's centre.
facts: Removing a part: (remaining weight)$\times GG'$ = (removed weight)$\times GG_1$, on opposite sides of $G$.

en.q: In how many years will a sum of ₹2,500 amount to ₹3,250 at 6% per annum simple interest?
en.explanation: Interest = ₹3,250 − ₹2,500 = ₹750. Interest for one year = 6% of ₹2,500 = ₹150. Time $= \frac{750}{150} = 5$ years.
notes: Yearly interest taken on the amount (₹195): $750 \div 195 \approx 3.8$.
That is the rate, not the time.
facts: $SI = \frac{PRT}{100}$, so $T = \frac{100 \times SI}{PR}$; simple interest is always on the principal.

en.q: The sum of a two-digit number and the number obtained by reversing its digits is 121. If the tens digit exceeds the units digit by 3, the number is:
en.explanation: Let the number be $10a + b$. Then $(10a + b) + (10b + a) = 11(a + b) = 121$, so $a + b = 11$; and $a - b = 3$. Hence $a = 7$, $b = 4$: the number is 74.
notes: That is the reversed number (units digit larger).
Digit sum 11, but the digits differ by 5.
Digit sum 11, but the digits differ by 1.
facts: A two-digit number with digits $a, b$ is $10a + b$; the number and its reverse add to $11(a + b)$ and differ by $9|a - b|$.

src.label: Expected TGT 5 · Q22 · asked in UP TGT 2003

en.q: One root of the equation $\begin{vmatrix}3x-8&3&3\\3&3x-8&3\\3&3&3x-8\end{vmatrix} = 0$ is:
en.explanation:
$C_1 \to C_1 + C_2 + C_3$ makes every entry of $C_1$ equal to $3x - 2$; take it out.
Then $R_2 - R_1$, $R_3 - R_1$ leave a triangular determinant: $(3x - 2)(3x - 11)^2 = 0$.
So $x = \frac23$ or $\frac{11}{3}$; among the options, $\frac23$.
notes: Makes the diagonal zero, but the determinant is then 54.
facts: If every row has the same sum, add all columns to the first and take that sum out.

en.q: Three forces $P$, $Q$, $R$ acting at a point are in equilibrium, and $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ are the angles between $Q$ and $R$, $R$ and $P$, $P$ and $Q$ respectively. By Lami's theorem:
en.explanation: Lami's theorem: if three concurrent forces are in equilibrium, each is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two: $\frac{P}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{Q}{\sin\beta} = \frac{R}{\sin\gamma}$.
notes: Angles paired with the wrong forces.
Each force is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two.
path: 15.2 Three forces in equilibrium: Lami's theorem
facts: Lami: $\frac{P}{\sin(\widehat{Q,R})} = \frac{Q}{\sin(\widehat{R,P})} = \frac{R}{\sin(\widehat{P,Q})}$.

en.q: If $x = \dfrac{\sqrt3 + 1}{\sqrt3 - 1}$, then $x + \dfrac1x$ equals:
en.explanation:
Rationalise: $x = \dfrac{(\sqrt3 + 1)^2}{3 - 1} = \dfrac{4 + 2\sqrt3}{2} = 2 + \sqrt3$, and $\dfrac1x = \dfrac{\sqrt3 - 1}{\sqrt3 + 1} = 2 - \sqrt3$.
So $x + \frac1x = 4$.
facts: $(2 + \sqrt3)(2 - \sqrt3) = 1$: these two are reciprocals.

en.q: The sum to infinity of the geometric series $a + ar + ar^2 + \dots$, where $|r| < 1$, is:
en.explanation: $S_n = \frac{a(1 - r^n)}{1 - r}$. For $|r| < 1$, $r^n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, so $S_\infty = \frac{a}{1 - r}$.
notes: That is the sum of the first $n$ terms.
That is the sum of $a - ar + ar^2 - \dots$ (ratio $-r$).
path: 1.6 Sequences and series: AP, GP, HP
facts: $S_\infty = \frac{a}{1 - r}$ exists only for $|r| < 1$; e.g. $1 + \frac12 + \frac14 + \dots = 2$.

en.q: In $\triangle ABC$, the bisector of $\angle A$ meets $BC$ at $D$. Then $BD : DC$ equals:
en.explanation: Angle-bisector theorem: $\frac{BD}{DC} = \frac{AB}{AC}$. Reason: triangles $ABD$ and $ADC$ have the same height from $A$, so their areas are as $BD : DC$; their areas are also $\frac12 AB \cdot AD\sin\frac A2 : \frac12 AC \cdot AD\sin\frac A2 = AB : AC$.
notes: Squares belong to other results (areas of similar triangles).
facts: Internal bisector of $\angle A$: $BD : DC = AB : AC = c : b$.

en.q: A set $N \subseteq \mathbb R$ is called a neighbourhood of a point $x \in \mathbb R$ if:
options: $N$ is a closed interval with $x$ as an end point
en.explanation: By definition $N$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ if $(x - \varepsilon, x + \varepsilon) \subseteq N$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$, i.e. $N$ contains an open interval containing $x$. Example: $[0, 2]$ is a neighbourhood of 1 but not of 0.
notes: $[0, 1]$ contains 0 but is not a neighbourhood of 0.
No open interval about an end point lies inside it.
A single point contains no open interval.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: A set is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of each of its points.

en.q: The diagonals of a parallelogram are $3\hat i + \hat j - 2\hat k$ and $\hat i - 3\hat j + 4\hat k$. The area of the parallelogram is:
en.explanation:
With diagonals $\vec d_1, \vec d_2$ the area is $\frac12|\vec d_1 \times \vec d_2|$.
$\vec d_1 \times \vec d_2 = \begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\3&1&-2\\1&-3&4\end{vmatrix} = -2\hat i - 14\hat j - 10\hat k$, of magnitude $\sqrt{4 + 196 + 100} = 10\sqrt3$.
Area $= \frac12 \times 10\sqrt3 = 5\sqrt3$ square units.
notes: $|\vec d_1 \times \vec d_2|$: that formula is for adjacent sides, not diagonals.
$\frac12|\vec d_1||\vec d_2|$: the sine of the angle is missing.
facts: Parallelogram: area $|\vec a \times \vec b|$ for adjacent sides, $\frac12|\vec d_1 \times \vec d_2|$ for diagonals.

en.q: A can do a piece of work in 12 days and B can do it in 18 days. They work together for 4 days, after which A leaves. In how many more days will B finish the remaining work?
en.explanation:
In one day A and B together do $\frac{1}{12} + \frac{1}{18} = \frac{5}{36}$ of the work. In 4 days: $\frac{20}{36} = \frac59$.
Left: $\frac49$. B alone needs $\frac49 \times 18 = 8$ days.
notes: Remaining $\frac49$ of the work at B's rate $\frac{1}{18}$ per day.
$\frac59 \times 18$: the part already done, not the part left.
Remaining work taken as $\frac13$ instead of $\frac49$.
facts: Work done = time × (sum of the daily rates); a rate is the reciprocal of the time for the whole work.

en.q: The value of $\begin{vmatrix}1&1&1\\1&1+x&1\\1&1&1+y\end{vmatrix}$ is:
en.explanation: $R_2 \to R_2 - R_1$ and $R_3 \to R_3 - R_1$ give $\begin{vmatrix}1&1&1\\0&x&0\\0&0&y\end{vmatrix}$, an upper triangular determinant, so its value is $1 \cdot x \cdot y = xy$.
notes: Diagonal entries added instead of multiplied.
Adds the 1 of the first row as well.
Product of the diagonal after $R_2 - R_1$, $R_3 - R_1$.
facts: Subtracting one row from another leaves a determinant unchanged; a triangular determinant is the product of its diagonal entries.

en.q: The general second-degree equation $ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0$ represents a pair of straight lines if:
en.explanation: The equation splits into two linear factors exactly when $\Delta = \begin{vmatrix}a&h&g\\h&b&f\\g&f&c\end{vmatrix} = abc + 2fgh - af^2 - bg^2 - ch^2 = 0$. If $\Delta \ne 0$ it is a proper conic (a parabola when $h^2 = ab$).
notes: With $\Delta \ne 0$ that is the condition for a parabola.
That makes the two lines perpendicular when $\Delta = 0$; it is not the condition itself.
$\Delta = 0$: the conic degenerates into two lines.
path: 11.3 General equation of the second degree
facts: $\Delta = abc + 2fgh - af^2 - bg^2 - ch^2$: $\Delta = 0$ pair of lines; $\Delta \ne 0$ with $h^2 = ab$, $h^2 < ab$, $h^2 > ab$: parabola, ellipse, hyperbola.

en.q: $\lim_{x\to0} \dfrac{3^x - 2^x}{x}$ is equal to:
en.explanation: Write $3^x - 2^x = (3^x - 1) - (2^x - 1)$. Since $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{a^x - 1}{x} = \log_e a$, the limit is $\log_e 3 - \log_e 2 = \log_e\frac32$. (Check by L'Hospital's rule: $3^x\log_e 3 - 2^x\log_e 2 \to \log_e 3 - \log_e 2$.)
notes: The two logarithms added instead of subtracted.
Subtracts the bases, $3 - 2$; the bases enter only through their logarithms.
The ratio of the bases without the logarithm.
facts: $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{a^x - 1}{x} = \log_e a$ ($a > 0$); for $a = e$ it is 1.

en.q: A sequence $\langle a_n\rangle$ of real numbers is said to converge to $l$ if:
options: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $m \in \mathbb N$ with $|a_n - l| < \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge m$
en.explanation: By definition $a_n \to l$ if, however small $\varepsilon > 0$ is, all the terms from some stage on lie in $(l - \varepsilon, l + \varepsilon)$. E.g. $\frac1n \to 0$: given $\varepsilon$, take $m > \frac1\varepsilon$.
notes: From some stage on, the terms stay within every $\varepsilon$ of $l$.
One fixed $\varepsilon$ only makes the sequence bounded.
$(-1)^n$ equals 1 infinitely often but does not converge.
$|a_n - l|$ may decrease to a positive number.
facts: A convergent sequence has exactly one limit and is bounded.

en.q: If $\sin A = \frac35$ and $\cos B = \frac{5}{13}$, where $A$ and $B$ are acute angles, then $\sin(A + B)$ equals:
en.explanation:
$\cos A = \frac45$, $\sin B = \frac{12}{13}$ (acute angles).
$\sin(A + B) = \sin A\cos B + \cos A\sin B = \frac35 \cdot \frac{5}{13} + \frac45 \cdot \frac{12}{13} = \frac{63}{65}$.
facts: $\sin(A \pm B) = \sin A\cos B \pm \cos A\sin B$.

en.q: A square matrix $A$ is called orthogonal if:
en.explanation: $A$ is orthogonal when $AA^T = A^TA = I$, i.e. $A^{-1} = A^T$; for example $\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}$. Taking determinants, $|A|^2 = 1$, so $|A| = \pm1$.
facts: Orthogonal: $AA^T = I$ and $|A| = \pm1$; symmetric: $A^T = A$; skew-symmetric: $A^T = -A$; involutory: $A^2 = I$.

src.label: Expected TGT 5 · Q36 · asked in UP TGT 2003

en.q: Two straight roads intersect at an angle of 60°. A bus on one road is 2 km away from the intersection and a car on the other road is 3 km away from the intersection. Then the direct distance between the two vehicles is:
en.explanation:
The bus, the car and the crossing form a triangle with sides 2 km and 3 km enclosing $60^\circ$.
$d^2 = 2^2 + 3^2 - 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cos 60^\circ = 13 - 6 = 7$, so $d = \sqrt7$ km.
notes: Too long: with $\cos 60^\circ$ the third side is $\sqrt7 \approx 2.65$ km.
Not given by any rule here.
Just $3 - 2$, as if on one line.
Cosine rule with the included angle $60^\circ$.
facts: Cosine rule: $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C$.

en.q: A homogeneous differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = f\left(\dfrac yx\right)$ is reduced to a separable equation by the substitution:
en.explanation: Put $y = vx$: then $\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}$, and the equation becomes $v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = f(v)$, i.e. $\frac{dv}{f(v) - v} = \frac{dx}{x}$, which is separable.
notes: Suits equations in $y - x$, not in $\frac yx$.
Does not remove the ratio $\frac yx$.
facts: Homogeneous $\frac{dy}{dx} = f\left(\frac yx\right)$: put $y = vx$; for $\frac{dy}{dx} = f(ax + by + c)$ put $v = ax + by + c$.

src.label: Expected TGT 5 · Q38 · asked in UP TGT 2001

en.q: The magnitudes of the vectors $\vec a, \vec b, \vec c$ are 3, 4, 5 respectively. If the vectors $\vec a, \vec b, \vec c$ are respectively perpendicular to the vectors $\vec b + \vec c$, $\vec c + \vec a$, $\vec a + \vec b$, then the magnitude of $\vec a + \vec b + \vec c$ will be:
en.explanation:
Adding $\vec a\cdot(\vec b + \vec c) = 0$, $\vec b\cdot(\vec c + \vec a) = 0$, $\vec c\cdot(\vec a + \vec b) = 0$ gives $2(\vec a\cdot\vec b + \vec b\cdot\vec c + \vec c\cdot\vec a) = 0$.
$|\vec a + \vec b + \vec c|^2 = 9 + 16 + 25 + 0 = 50$, so the magnitude is $5\sqrt2$.
facts: $|\vec a + \vec b + \vec c|^2 = |\vec a|^2 + |\vec b|^2 + |\vec c|^2 + 2(\vec a\cdot\vec b + \vec b\cdot\vec c + \vec c\cdot\vec a)$.

en.q: For the conic $\dfrac{l}{r} = 1 + e\cos\theta$ (focus at the pole), the length of the latus rectum is:
en.explanation: The latus rectum is the focal chord perpendicular to the axis, along $\theta = \pm\frac\pi2$. There $\cos\theta = 0$, so $r = l$ on each side: the length is $2l$ ($l$ is the semi-latus rectum).
notes: That is the distance from the focus to the directrix.
path: 11.8 Polar equation of a conic; common tangents (PGT)
facts: In $\frac lr = 1 + e\cos\theta$: semi-latus rectum $l$, distance from focus to directrix $\frac le$.

en.q: If $n(A) = 3$ and $n(B) = 2$, then the number of relations from $A$ to $B$ is:
en.explanation: A relation from $A$ to $B$ is any subset of $A \times B$, which has $3 \times 2 = 6$ elements. The number of subsets is $2^6 = 64$.
facts: Relations from $A$ to $B$: $2^{mn}$; functions from $A$ to $B$: $n^m$ (with $m = n(A)$, $n = n(B)$).

en.q: The number of points at which the function $f(x) = |x - 0.5| + |x - 1| + \tan x$ does not have derivative in the interval $[0, 2]$ is:
en.explanation:
$|x - 0.5|$ has a corner at $x = 0.5$ and $|x - 1|$ a corner at $x = 1$; there the one-sided derivatives differ by 2.
$\tan x$ is not defined at $x = \frac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.571 \in [0, 2]$, so $f$ has no derivative there either.
Elsewhere all terms are differentiable. Total: 3 points.
notes: Counts the two corners but forgets that $\tan x$ is undefined at $\frac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.57$.
No fourth point: $\tan x$ is smooth elsewhere in $[0, 2]$.
facts: $|x - a|$ has a corner at $x = a$; a function has no derivative where it is not even defined.

en.q: If $\omega$ is an imaginary cube root of unity, then the value of $(1 + \omega + \omega^2)(1 - \omega + \omega^2)$ is:
en.explanation: For an imaginary cube root of unity $1 + \omega + \omega^2 = 0$, so the product is $0 \times (1 - \omega + \omega^2) = 0$. (The second factor is $-2\omega$, which is not zero.)
path: 10.4 Polar form, Euler's form and De Moivre's theorem
facts: $1 + \omega + \omega^2 = 0$ and $\omega^3 = 1$; hence $1 - \omega + \omega^2 = -2\omega$ and $1 + \omega - \omega^2 = -2\omega^2$.

en.q: $\sin C + \sin D$ is equal to:
en.explanation: Put $C = A + B$, $D = A - B$ in $\sin(A + B) + \sin(A - B) = 2\sin A\cos B$. Then $A = \frac{C + D}{2}$ and $B = \frac{C - D}{2}$, so $\sin C + \sin D = 2\sin\frac{C + D}{2}\cos\frac{C - D}{2}$.
facts: The four $C$–$D$ formulas come from adding and subtracting the compound-angle formulas.

en.q: If $\sin y = x\sin(a + y)$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ is equal to:
en.explanation:
Make $x$ the subject: $x = \dfrac{\sin y}{\sin(a + y)}$. Differentiate with respect to $y$ (quotient rule):
$$\frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{\cos y\sin(a + y) - \sin y\cos(a + y)}{\sin^2(a + y)} = \frac{\sin\big((a + y) - y\big)}{\sin^2(a + y)} = \frac{\sin a}{\sin^2(a + y)}.$$
Hence $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{dx/dy} = \dfrac{\sin^2(a + y)}{\sin a}$.
notes: The square in the numerator is lost.
Neither the square nor the factor $\frac{1}{\sin a}$.
facts: If $x$ is easy to isolate, find $\frac{dx}{dy}$ and invert: $\frac{dy}{dx} = 1\big/\frac{dx}{dy}$; the numerator collapses by $\sin(A - B) = \sin A\cos B - \cos A\sin B$.

en.q: The equation of the tangent plane at the point $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ of the sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = a^2$ is:
en.explanation: The radius to $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ has direction ratios $x_1, y_1, z_1$ and is normal to the tangent plane: $x_1(x - x_1) + y_1(y - y_1) + z_1(z - z_1) = 0$, i.e. $xx_1 + yy_1 + zz_1 = x_1^2 + y_1^2 + z_1^2 = a^2$.
notes: Does not depend on the point of contact.
The parallel plane through the centre.
The radius is normal to the tangent plane.
A sphere of radius $a$ centred at the point, not a plane.
facts: Tangent plane to $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = a^2$ at $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$: $xx_1 + yy_1 + zz_1 = a^2$ (as for the tangent to a circle).

en.q: If the position vector of $A$ is $\hat i + 2\hat j - \hat k$ and $\overrightarrow{AB} = 2\hat i - \hat j + 3\hat k$, then the position vector of $B$ is:
en.explanation: $\overrightarrow{AB} = \vec b - \vec a$, so $\vec b = \vec a + \overrightarrow{AB} = (1 + 2)\hat i + (2 - 1)\hat j + (-1 + 3)\hat k = 3\hat i + \hat j + 2\hat k$.
notes: Halved, as if a mid-point were wanted.
facts: $\overrightarrow{AB} = \vec b - \vec a$: position vector of the head minus that of the tail.

en.q: The sum of all the binomial coefficients ${}^nC_0 + {}^nC_1 + {}^nC_2 + \dots + {}^nC_n$ is:
en.explanation: Put $x = 1$ in $(1 + x)^n = {}^nC_0 + {}^nC_1x + \dots + {}^nC_nx^n$: the sum is $(1 + 1)^n = 2^n$.
notes: That is the sum of the odd-place (or of the even-place) coefficients.
Grows too slowly: for $n = 3$ the sum is $1 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 8$, not 9.

en.q: The multiplicative inverse of the complex number $3 + 4i$ is:
notes: $\frac{z}{|z|^2}$: the conjugate is missing; its product with $3 + 4i$ is $\frac{-7 + 24i}{25}$, not 1.
Only the conjugate: $(3 + 4i)(3 - 4i) = 25$, so it must still be divided by 25.
Sign of the real part wrong: $(3 + 4i)\cdot\frac{-3 + 4i}{25} = -1$.
facts: $(a + ib)^{-1} = \dfrac{a - ib}{a^2 + b^2}$ for $a + ib \ne 0$.

en.q: The domain of the function $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{|x| - x}}$ is:
en.explanation: Need $|x| - x > 0$. For $x \ge 0$, $|x| - x = 0$ (not allowed). For $x < 0$, $|x| - x = -2x > 0$. So the domain is $(-\infty, 0)$.
facts: $|x| - x = 0$ for $x \ge 0$ and $= -2x$ for $x < 0$.

en.q: In how many ways can 6 different prizes be given to 3 students, if a student may receive any number of prizes?
en.explanation: Each of the 6 prizes can go to any of the 3 students, independently: $3^6 = 729$ ways.
notes: $6 \times 3$: the choices added up instead of multiplied.
${}^6P_3$: as if each student got exactly one prize.
facts: Distributing $n$ different objects among $r$ people without restriction: $r^n$ ways.

en.q: For $a > 0$, $a \ne 1$ and $x > 0$, $a^{\log_a x}$ equals:
en.explanation: $\log_a x$ is the power to which $a$ must be raised to give $x$; so raising $a$ to that power gives $x$. E.g. $2^{\log_2 8} = 2^3 = 8$.
notes: The exponent itself, not the power.
facts: $a^{\log_a x} = x$ and $\log_a a^x = x$; $\log_a 1 = 0$, $\log_a a = 1$.

en.q: For the parabola $y^2 = 4ax$, the length of the subnormal at any point is:
en.explanation: $2y\frac{dy}{dx} = 4a$, so $y\frac{dy}{dx} = 2a$. Subnormal $= \left|y\frac{dy}{dx}\right| = 2a$, the same at every point. (The subtangent is $\left|\frac{y}{dy/dx}\right| = \frac{y^2}{2a} = 2x$.)
facts: Subtangent $= \left|\frac{y}{y'}\right|$, subnormal $= |yy'|$; for $y^2 = 4ax$ the subnormal is the constant $2a$.

en.q: The angle in a semicircle is:
en.explanation: The diameter subtends $180^\circ$ at the centre; the angle at any point of the remaining arc is half of it, $90^\circ$ (Thales).
notes: Angles in a major segment are acute.
$180^\circ$ is the angle at the centre, not on the circle.
Half of the $180^\circ$ arc at the centre.
Angles in a minor segment are obtuse.
facts: Angle at the centre = 2 × angle on the circle on the same arc; so the angle in a semicircle is $90^\circ$.

en.q: For $-1 \le x \le 1$, $\cos^{-1}(-x)$ is equal to:
en.explanation: If $\cos^{-1}x = \theta \in [0, \pi]$, then $\cos(\pi - \theta) = -x$ and $\pi - \theta \in [0, \pi]$, so $\cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1}x$. E.g. $\cos^{-1}\left(-\frac12\right) = \pi - \frac\pi3 = \frac{2\pi}{3}$.
notes: That rule holds for $\sin^{-1}$ and $\tan^{-1}$, not for $\cos^{-1}$.
Can exceed $\pi$, outside the principal range.

en.q: If $a_1 = \sqrt2$ and $a_{n+1} = \sqrt{2 + a_n}$ for $n \ge 1$, then $\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n$ is:
en.explanation: By induction $0 < a_n < 2$ (if $a_n < 2$, then $a_{n+1} < \sqrt4 = 2$), and $a_{n+1} > a_n$ because $a_n^2 - a_n - 2 = (a_n - 2)(a_n + 1) < 0$, i.e. $a_n^2 < 2 + a_n$. So the sequence is increasing and bounded above, hence convergent. Its limit $L \ge \sqrt2$ satisfies $L = \sqrt{2 + L}$, i.e. $L^2 - L - 2 = 0$, $(L - 2)(L + 1) = 0$, so $L = 2$.
notes: That is the first term; the sequence increases.
The other root of $L^2 - L - 2 = 0$; impossible, as every term is positive.
Correct: the positive root of $L = \sqrt{2 + L}$.
The sequence increases but stays below 2, so it is bounded and converges.
facts: A monotonic increasing sequence that is bounded above converges; for $a_{n+1} = f(a_n)$ find the limit from $L = f(L)$ and keep the root that fits the terms.

en.q: For a given velocity of projection, the horizontal range on a horizontal plane is maximum when the angle of projection is:
en.explanation: $R = \frac{u^2\sin 2\alpha}{g}$ is greatest when $\sin2\alpha = 1$, i.e. $\alpha = 45^\circ$; then $R_{\max} = \frac{u^2}{g}$.
notes: Gives the same range as $60^\circ$, less than at $45^\circ$.
facts: Angles $\alpha$ and $90^\circ - \alpha$ give equal ranges; the maximum range $\frac{u^2}{g}$ is at $45^\circ$.

en.q: The angles of elevation of the top of a tower from two points on the ground, at distances $a$ and $b$ from its foot along the same straight line, are complementary. The height of the tower is:
en.explanation: If the angles are $\theta$ and $90^\circ - \theta$, then $\tan\theta = \frac ha$ and $\tan(90^\circ - \theta) = \cot\theta = \frac hb$. Multiplying, $1 = \frac{h^2}{ab}$, so $h = \sqrt{ab}$.
notes: The arithmetic mean; the height is the geometric mean.
No right angle joins these lengths.
facts: Complementary angles of elevation from distances $a$ and $b$: height $= \sqrt{ab}$.

en.q: The locus of the centre of a circle which touches externally the circle $x^2 + y^2 - 6x - 6y + 14 = 0$ and also touches the $y$-axis is given by the equation:
en.explanation:
The given circle has centre $(3, 3)$ and radius $\sqrt{9 + 9 - 14} = 2$. A circle with centre $(h, k)$ touching the $y$-axis has radius $|h|$; here $h > 0$.
External contact: $(h - 3)^2 + (k - 3)^2 = (h + 2)^2 \Rightarrow k^2 - 10h - 6k + 14 = 0$.
Locus: $y^2 - 10x - 6y + 14 = 0$.
notes: Should be quadratic in $y$, since the circle touches the $y$-axis.
facts: Circles touch externally when the distance between centres equals the sum of the radii.

src.label: Expected TGT 5 · Q59 · asked in UP TGT 2003

en.q: If the three lines $x + y = 1$, $x - y = 5$ and $2x + 3y = k$ are concurrent, then the value of $k$ is:
en.explanation: $x + y = 1$ and $x - y = 5$ meet at $(3, -2)$. The third line passes through it: $k = 2(3) + 3(-2) = 0$.
facts: Three lines are concurrent when the third passes through the meet of the other two.

en.q: The points representing the three cube roots of unity in the Argand plane are the vertices of:
en.explanation: The roots $1, \omega, \omega^2$ are $e^{0}$, $e^{2\pi i/3}$, $e^{4\pi i/3}$: on the unit circle, $120^\circ$ apart. Equal arcs give equal chords (each $\sqrt3$), so the triangle is equilateral, with centroid at the origin since $1 + \omega + \omega^2 = 0$.
notes: Three points $120^\circ$ apart on the unit circle.
$120^\circ$ is the angle at the centre, not at a vertex.
path: 10.4 Polar form, Euler's form and De Moivre's theorem
facts: The $n$th roots of unity are the vertices of a regular $n$-gon inscribed in the unit circle.

en.q: The general solution of the equation $\tan^2\alpha + 2\sqrt3\tan\alpha = 1$ is:
en.explanation:
$1 - \tan^2\alpha = 2\sqrt3\tan\alpha$ (and $\tan^2\alpha \ne 1$, else $\tan\alpha = 0$), so
$$\tan 2\alpha = \frac{2\tan\alpha}{1 - \tan^2\alpha} = \frac{1}{\sqrt3} \Rightarrow 2\alpha = n\pi + \frac{\pi}{6}.$$
Hence $\alpha = \frac{n\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{12} = (6n + 1)\frac{\pi}{12}$. (Directly: $\tan\alpha = 2 - \sqrt3$ or $-2 - \sqrt3$, i.e. $15^\circ$ or $105^\circ$ plus multiples of $180^\circ$.)
notes: $\tan\alpha$ is undefined at odd multiples of $\frac{\pi}{2}$.
facts: Spot $\tan 2\alpha = \frac{2\tan\alpha}{1 - \tan^2\alpha}$ in a quadratic in $\tan\alpha$.

en.q: The opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are:
en.explanation: Opposite angles stand on arcs that together make the whole circle, so their sum is $\frac12 \times 360^\circ = 180^\circ$.
notes: Equal only for special shapes such as a rectangle.
facts: In a cyclic quadrilateral $\angle A + \angle C = \angle B + \angle D = 180^\circ$; an exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle.

src.label: Expected TGT 5 · Q63 · asked in UP TGT 2003

en.q: The set of values of $p$ for which the roots of the equation $3x^2 + 2x + p(p - 1) = 0$ are of opposite sign is:
en.explanation: Roots of opposite sign means a negative product: $\frac{p(p - 1)}{3} < 0 \Rightarrow 0 < p < 1$. (A negative product also makes the discriminant $4 - 12p(p - 1)$ positive, so the roots are real.)
notes: Includes $p \ge 1$, where the product is not negative.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: For $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$: roots of opposite sign $\iff \frac ca < 0$ (then they are real automatically).

facts: De Morgan: $(A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'$.

en.q: In any group, the order of an element $a$ and the order of its inverse $a^{-1}$ are:
options: equal only when the group is abelian
en.explanation: $(a^{-1})^n = (a^n)^{-1}$, so $a^n = e$ exactly when $(a^{-1})^n = e$. The least such $n$ is the same: $o(a^{-1}) = o(a)$.
facts: $o(a) = o(a^{-1}) = o(gag^{-1})$ in every group.

en.q: If $A = \begin{bmatrix}2&0&0\\0&3&0\\0&0&4\end{bmatrix}$, then $A^{-1}$ is:
en.explanation: $|A| = 24 \ne 0$ and $\operatorname{adj}A = \begin{bmatrix}12&0&0\\0&8&0\\0&0&6\end{bmatrix}$, so $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{24}\operatorname{adj}A$, the diagonal matrix of the reciprocals $\frac12, \frac13, \frac14$.
facts: $\operatorname{diag}(a, b, c)^{-1} = \operatorname{diag}\left(\frac1a, \frac1b, \frac1c\right)$ for $abc \ne 0$; in general $A^{-1} = \frac{\operatorname{adj}A}{|A|}$.

en.q: $\int \operatorname{cosec} x\,dx$ equals:
en.explanation: $\frac{d}{dx}\log|\operatorname{cosec} x - \cot x| = \frac{-\operatorname{cosec} x\cot x + \operatorname{cosec}^2x}{\operatorname{cosec} x - \cot x} = \operatorname{cosec} x$. Equivalently $\int\operatorname{cosec} x\,dx = \log\left|\tan\frac x2\right| + C$.
notes: That is the derivative of $\operatorname{cosec} x$.
facts: $\int\sec x\,dx = \log|\sec x + \tan x| + C$; $\int\operatorname{cosec} x\,dx = \log|\operatorname{cosec} x - \cot x| + C$.

en.q: The rank of the matrix $\begin{bmatrix}8&1&3&6\\0&3&2&2\\-8&-1&-3&4\end{bmatrix}$ will be:
en.explanation: $R_3 \to R_3 + R_1$ gives $(0, 0, 0, 10)$. The rows $(8, 1, 3, 6)$, $(0, 3, 2, 2)$, $(0, 0, 0, 10)$ are in echelon form with three non-zero rows, so the rank is 3 (the most a matrix with 3 rows can have).
notes: $R_3$ is not a combination of $R_1$ and $R_2$ (its last entry differs).
Three non-zero rows in echelon form.
A $3 \times 4$ matrix has rank at most 3.
Rank 1 would need every row to be a multiple of one row.
path: 2.4 Rank and systems of linear equations
facts: Rank = number of non-zero rows of an echelon form; the rank of an $m \times n$ matrix is at most $\min(m, n)$.

en.q: If two forces $P$ and $Q$ act at a point at an angle $\alpha$, the magnitude $R$ of their resultant is given by:
en.explanation: By the parallelogram law, $R^2 = P^2 + Q^2 + 2PQ\cos\alpha$; check: $\alpha = 0$ gives $R = P + Q$, $\alpha = 180^\circ$ gives $|P - Q|$.
facts: $R^2 = P^2 + Q^2 + 2PQ\cos\alpha$, $\tan\theta = \frac{Q\sin\alpha}{P + Q\cos\alpha}$ (angle with $P$).

en.q: The total number of 9 digit numbers which have all different digits is:
en.explanation:
The first digit can be any of 1–9 (not 0): 9 ways. The remaining 8 places are filled from the 9 digits left, in order: $^9P_8 = 9!$ ways.
Total $= 9 \times 9!$. (Equivalently $^{10}P_9 - {}^9P_8 = 10! - 9! = 9 \times 9!$.)
notes: Larger than $10!$, which already counts every arrangement of 9 different digits, leading 0 included.
9 choices for the first digit, then $^9P_8 = 9!$ for the rest.
Forgets that 0 may be used after the first place.
facts: Leading digit cannot be 0: count it first, then arrange the rest.

en.q: According to the work–energy principle, the work done by the resultant force on a body equals the change in its:
en.explanation: Work–energy principle: $W_{\text{net}} = \frac12mv^2 - \frac12mu^2$, the change in kinetic energy.
notes: Potential energy changes by the work done against gravity, not by the work of the resultant force.
Change of momentum equals the impulse.
facts: Work = change in KE; impulse = change in momentum.

en.q: The particles A and B are dropped from the heights of 5 m and 20 m respectively. Then the ratio of time taken by A to that taken by B, to reach the ground is:
en.explanation: From rest, $h = \frac12 gt^2$, so $t = \sqrt{2h/g} \propto \sqrt h$. $t_A : t_B = \sqrt5 : \sqrt{20} = 1 : 2$.
notes: Ratio of the heights, not of the times.
path: 15.8 Rectilinear motion and simple harmonic motion
facts: Free fall from rest: $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$.

en.q: $\int_0^{\pi} \frac{x\sin x}{1 + \cos^2 x}\,dx$ equals:
en.explanation:
Replace $x$ by $\pi - x$: $I = \int_0^{\pi}\frac{(\pi - x)\sin x}{1 + \cos^2x}dx$. Adding,
$$2I = \pi\int_0^{\pi}\frac{\sin x}{1 + \cos^2x}dx = \pi\left[-\tan^{-1}(\cos x)\right]_0^{\pi} = \pi\left(\frac\pi4 + \frac\pi4\right) = \frac{\pi^2}{2}.$$
So $I = \frac{\pi^2}{4}$.
notes: The factor $\pi$ from the King's-rule step dropped.
facts: $\int_0^a f(x)\,dx = \int_0^a f(a - x)\,dx$; with $x\,g(\sin x)$ on $[0, \pi]$ it gives $\frac\pi2\int_0^\pi g(\sin x)\,dx$.

en.q: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(a^x\right)$, where $a > 0$, equals:
en.explanation: $a^x = e^{x\log_e a}$, so $\frac{d}{dx}a^x = e^{x\log_e a}\cdot\log_e a = a^x\log_e a$.
notes: Power rule wrongly applied to a variable exponent.
facts: $\frac{d}{dx}a^x = a^x\log_e a$; $\int a^x\,dx = \frac{a^x}{\log_e a} + C$.

en.q: If $S$ and $S'$ are the foci of the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ $(a > b)$ and $P$ is any point on the ellipse, then $SP + S'P$ equals:
en.explanation: For $P(x_1, y_1)$ on the ellipse, $SP = e \times$ (distance of $P$ from the directrix $x = \frac ae$) $= e\left(\frac ae - x_1\right) = a - ex_1$, and in the same way $S'P = a + ex_1$. Adding, $SP + S'P = 2a$, the length of the major axis, the same for every point $P$.
notes: That is the length of the minor axis.
That is the distance $SS'$ between the foci.
That is the distance between the two directrices.
facts: Focal distances of $(x_1, y_1)$ on $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$: $a \mp ex_1$; their sum is the major axis $2a$.

en.q: The hyperbola conjugate to $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ is:
en.explanation: The conjugate hyperbola has the transverse and conjugate axes interchanged: $\frac{y^2}{b^2} - \frac{x^2}{a^2} = 1$. The two share the asymptotes $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 0$, and their eccentricities satisfy $\frac{1}{e_1^2} + \frac{1}{e_2^2} = 1$.
notes: Another hyperbola along the $x$-axis ($a$ and $b$ swapped).
That is the pair of asymptotes.
facts: A hyperbola and its conjugate have the same asymptotes, and $e_1^{-2} + e_2^{-2} = 1$.

en.q: The vector $\vec a$ lies in the plane of vectors $\vec b$ and $\vec c$; which of the following is correct?
en.explanation: $\vec b \times \vec c$ is perpendicular to the plane of $\vec b$ and $\vec c$, hence to $\vec a$; so $\vec a\cdot(\vec b \times \vec c) = 0$ (the parallelepiped is flat).
notes: Coplanar vectors have zero scalar triple product.
facts: $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c] = 0 \iff \vec a, \vec b, \vec c$ are coplanar.

en.q: If $x$ lies in the interval $[0, 1]$, then the minimum value of $x^2 + x + 1$ is:
en.explanation: $f'(x) = 2x + 1 > 0$ on $[0, 1]$, so $f$ is increasing there and its least value is $f(0) = 1$.
notes: The expression is never 0 (no real roots).
facts: On a closed interval compare end-point values with stationary points inside the interval only.

en.q: A uniform beam $AB$, 4 m long and weighing 60 N, rests horizontally on two supports at its ends $A$ and $B$. A load of 40 N is placed on it 1 m from $A$. The reaction at $A$ is:
en.explanation: Moments about $B$: $R_A \times 4 = 60 \times 2 + 40 \times 3 = 240$, so $R_A = 60$ N. Then $R_B = 100 - 60 = 40$ N.
notes: Half the total load: the position of the 40 N ignored.
path: 15.3 Coplanar forces, moments and parallel forces
facts: For a beam on two supports, take moments about one support to find the other reaction.

en.q: The sum of the first $n$ natural numbers is $\frac15$ times the sum of their squares; then the value of $n$ is:
en.explanation:
$$\frac{n(n+1)}{2} = \frac15 \cdot \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} \Rightarrow 2n + 1 = 15 \Rightarrow n = 7.$$
Check: $1 + \dots + 7 = 28$ and $1^2 + \dots + 7^2 = 140 = 5 \times 28$.
path: 1.6 Sequences and series: AP, GP, HP
facts: $\dfrac{\sum n}{\sum n^2} = \dfrac{3}{2n + 1}$.

en.q: In a metric space $(X, d)$, the triangle inequality states that for all $x, y, z \in X$:
en.explanation: The metric axioms: $d(x, y) \ge 0$ with equality iff $x = y$; $d(x, y) = d(y, x)$; and the triangle inequality $d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)$. In $\mathbb R$ with $d(x, y) = |x - y|$ it reads $|x - z| \le |x - y| + |y - z|$.
notes: Equality holds only in special positions (e.g. $y$ between $x$ and $z$ on $\mathbb R$).
One side of a triangle is at most the sum of the other two.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: A metric: $d(x, y) \ge 0$, $d(x, y) = 0 \iff x = y$, symmetry, triangle inequality.

en.q: Every subgroup of a cyclic group is:
en.explanation: If $G = \langle a\rangle$ and $H \ne \{e\}$ is a subgroup, let $m$ be the least positive integer with $a^m \in H$; division with remainder shows $H = \langle a^m\rangle$. So every subgroup is cyclic.
notes: A cyclic group is abelian, so are its subgroups.
False: $\mathbb Z_6$ is a subgroup of itself, of order 6.
Generated by its least positive power of the generator.
facts: A cyclic group of order $n$ has exactly one subgroup of each order $d \mid n$, and each is cyclic.

en.q: The mean deviation of a set of observations is least when the deviations are taken from the:
en.explanation: $\sum|x_i - a|$ is smallest when $a$ is the median. E.g. for 1, 2, 9: about the median 2 the sum is $1 + 0 + 7 = 8$; about the mean 4 it is $3 + 2 + 5 = 10$.
notes: The mean minimises the sum of squared deviations, not of absolute deviations.
facts: $\sum|x_i - a|$ is least for $a$ = median; $\sum(x_i - a)^2$ is least for $a$ = mean.

en.q: If one root of the equation $x^2 - 6x + k = 0$ is double the other, then $k$ equals:
en.explanation: Let the roots be $\alpha$ and $2\alpha$. Sum: $3\alpha = 6$, so $\alpha = 2$; product: $k = \alpha \cdot 2\alpha = 2\alpha^2 = 8$ (roots 2 and 4).
notes: Equal roots (zero discriminant), not roots in the ratio 1 : 2.
That is the sum of the roots.
$2\alpha = 6$ used for the sum: roots 3 and 6.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: For roots in a given ratio, write them as $\alpha$ and $k\alpha$ and use the sum and the product.

en.q: A letter is chosen at random from the letters of the word MATHEMATICS. The probability that it is a vowel is:
en.explanation: MATHEMATICS has 11 letters; the vowels are A, E, A, I, i.e. 4 letters. P(vowel) $= \frac{4}{11}$.
notes: That is the probability of a consonant.
Distinct vowels over distinct letters: repeated letters must be counted.
path: 16.1 Basic probability and the addition theorem
facts: Classical probability = favourable ÷ total equally likely outcomes; repeated letters count separately.

en.q: The median of the numbers 50, 48, 47, 48.5, 50.5, 52, 48.8, 46 will be:
en.explanation: In ascending order: 46, 47, 48, 48.5, 48.8, 50, 50.5, 52. Here $n = 8$ is even, so the median is the mean of the 4th and 5th values: $\frac{48.5 + 48.8}{2} = 48.65$.
notes: 50 is the 6th ordered value (or the first number as listed).
Mean of the 4th and 5th ordered values.
Only the 4th ordered value; for even $n$ the two middle values are averaged.
facts: For even $n$, median $= \frac12\left[\left(\frac n2\right)\text{th} + \left(\frac n2 + 1\right)\text{th}\right]$ ordered values.

en.q: By Cantor's theorem, for every set $A$:
options: $A$ and its power set $P(A)$ have the same cardinality
$P(A)$ has exactly twice as many elements as $A$
the cardinality of $P(A)$ is greater than that of $A$
en.explanation: $a \mapsto \{a\}$ maps $A$ one-one into $P(A)$, so $|A| \le |P(A)|$. No map $f: A \to P(A)$ is onto: the set $B = \{a \in A : a \notin f(a)\}$ differs from every $f(a)$. Hence $|P(A)| > |A|$; e.g. $P(\mathbb N)$ is uncountable.
notes: For finite $A$ with $n$ elements, $P(A)$ has $2^n$, not $2n$.
$\mathbb N$ is countable but $P(\mathbb N)$ is not.
facts: Cantor: $|P(A)| > |A|$; for a finite set of $n$ elements $|P(A)| = 2^n$; $P(\mathbb N)$ has the cardinality $c$ of $\mathbb R$.

en.q: A person draws a card from a pack of 52 cards and puts it back in the pack. He continues doing this until he gets a spade. What is the probability that he fails to draw a spade the first two times and draws a spade the third time?
en.explanation:
With replacement the draws are independent, and $P(\text{spade}) = \frac{13}{52} = \frac14$ each time.
P(no spade, no spade, spade) $= \frac34 \cdot \frac34 \cdot \frac14 = \frac{9}{64}$.
(Given that the first two draws failed, the chance of a spade on the third alone would still be $\frac14$: the draws are independent.)
path: 16.2 Conditional probability, multiplication theorem, independent events
facts: For independent events $P(A \cap B \cap C) = P(A)P(B)P(C)$.

en.q: The parametric coordinates of a point on the parabola $y^2 = 12x$ are:
en.explanation: $y^2 = 12x = 4 \cdot 3 \cdot x$, so $a = 3$ and the point is $(at^2, 2at) = (3t^2, 6t)$. Check: $(6t)^2 = 36t^2 = 12 \times 3t^2$.
facts: $y^2 = 4ax$: point $(at^2, 2at)$, tangent $ty = x + at^2$, focus $(a, 0)$, directrix $x = -a$.

en.q: A vector whose initial point is not fixed, so that it may be moved parallel to itself anywhere, is called a:
en.explanation: A free vector is fixed only by its magnitude and direction; its initial point may be anywhere. A position vector has its initial point at the origin; a localised vector is tied to a line of action.
notes: A null vector has zero magnitude.
A position vector starts at the origin.
A localised vector has a fixed line of action.
facts: Free vector: initial point arbitrary; localised vector: tied to a line; position vector: from the origin.
